input: Please explain your motivations for pursuing a career as a commercial solicitor and why you think Norton Rose Fulbright would be a good match for you (Maximum 750 words).
output:
Commercial law first became compelling while I was at Schroders, where my team led compliance work on new European sustainability regulations. Even after we had worked through a 200-page consultation paper, the directors remained unsure what the rules meant for our funds. Progress accelerated only when City external counsel distilled the changes that actually affected our business. Their clarity and bespoke advice impressed me enough that I began seriously considering a solicitor career.

Insight schemes at Paul Hastings, Baker McKenzie and Vinson & Elkins confirmed that interest. On an international joint-venture case study I found myself weaving Russian foreign-policy analysis and private-equity knowledge into legal submissions. That mix of topical, cross-disciplinary reasoning suited someone with broad academic curiosity far more than the heavily quantitative demands of my previous role. Practising law would let me deepen my interest in business and finance while drawing on strengths built as a History and International Relations graduate.

Norton Rose Fulbright’s multicultural setting is the foremost reason I applied. At the Energy Transition event, senior associate Melusi Dlamini explained how the firm’s international footprint enabled African energy work that matched personal interests. As a Hongkonger educated at an international school representing more than 80 nationalities, I am motivated by collaboration across regions. Living with roommates from Bulgaria, Timor-Leste and Mauritius taught me to value contrasting perspectives on global questions. A global firm would both use and stretch that cultural fluency, including when building rapport with international clients—especially on an international secondment.

I am equally drawn to Norton Rose Fulbright’s industry model, particularly in energy. Energy case studies and conversations with project-finance lawyers at Vinson & Elkins showed me how tangible the work can feel. Partner Amy Armitage made a similar point: seeing the physical sites behind mandates was highly rewarding. An industry-focused structure lets trainees learn from deep sector specialists and follow matters across the project lifecycle. Practice groups that hold not only local accolades but also global Band 1 rankings for multi-jurisdictional work make Norton Rose Fulbright an ideal place to test possible qualification specialisms within an international firm.

I also bring competencies that commercial practice requires. I can break down dense material and surface useful insights: I authored a monthly firmwide briefing on the cross-border retail fund market that the CEO regularly engaged with, pulling salient points from large datasets, identifying top-selling sectors and funds, and explaining trends and outliers through macroeconomic analysis. That analytical standard underpins legal work. I also take initiative to learn and support colleagues. When my manager was on secondment and available only Mondays and Fridays, I mastered the datasets and slides updated for the Sustainability ExCo so mid-week queries would not stall. When the Chief Investment Officer made urgent requests, I could respond and back the team. I welcome greater responsibility and look for ways to help.

Resilience as a self-starter matters too. My BlackRock internship became virtual during Covid, with an eight-hour time difference while I was in Hong Kong. Determined not to fall behind economics students who already knew more finance, I pursued every available route—coffee chats with 30 people across geographies and functions, plus self-study for the Bloomberg Market Concepts certification. That grit is what I would bring to the high-stakes setting of a global firm such as Norton Rose Fulbright.
